sections.heading: Listen before you move
sections.player_question: Listen before you move
sections.case_text: Suzy Says builds its tension around a simple problem: hearing an instruction does not always mean you should act on it. A smiling host addresses you through a television, and a colorful floor mat gives ordinary movements a precise meaning. The familiar presentation makes it tempting to react as soon as you recognize a color or an action. Identify the qualifying words and requested action before moving, then respond within the time shown by the current task.

sections.heading: The first command round
sections.player_question: The first command round
sections.case_text: The qualifying Suzy says words are the decision you make before choosing a destination. When the host uses those words to give an instruction, carry out the requested action. When that qualification is missing, do not perform the requested action merely because you recognize its target. The opening practice draws attention to missing qualifying words, so listen for that distinction before matching an action to the room.

sections.heading: Keep a map of the ordinary house
sections.player_question: Keep a map of the ordinary house
sections.case_text: This is why memorizing only a list of keys is not enough. You are connecting language to a physical state: where you stand, what you face and which object you reach. If you are uncertain after a mistake, reconstruct those parts separately. You may have understood the noun but reacted to an unqualified line, performed the right movement in the wrong place, or become distracted before the instruction finished.

sections.heading: Separate a mistake from a technical problem
sections.player_question: Separate a mistake from a technical problem
sections.case_text: A scare or sharp change in presentation does not by itself prove that a key failed. The game uses uncertainty to put pressure on an otherwise small control set. Before changing browser settings, remember the instruction, its prefix and your position. If you obeyed an unqualified command, that is a different problem from a movement key that never reaches the player.

sections.heading: An ordinary questionnaire becomes uncomfortable
sections.player_question: An ordinary questionnaire becomes uncomfortable
sections.case_text: Please Answer Carefully begins as a modest online questionnaire. You select responses about everyday internet habits, move through a familiar form and gradually find the questions becoming less impersonal. The horror lives in that change of relationship: a screen that initially asks for information starts to feel as though it expects something from you. There is no house to explore or enemy to outrun. Your attention stays on wording, choices and sound.

sections.player_question: Select an option, then use the arrow
sections.case_text: The title screen uses the same selection-and-continue language as the survey itself. Choose Begin game, then use the arrow that appears. sections.player_question: Checkboxes, response circles and the hours slider
sections.case_text: The early questions teach three slightly different interactions. The device question allows multiple selections, so tick the options you want and then continue. The question about time spent online uses a slider. Later questions present a set of alternative responses. Read the instruction attached to each question instead of assuming every screen accepts the same kind of answer.

sections.player_question: A missing arrow does not always mean a broken game
sections.case_text: If you cannot continue, first identify which kind of page is open. On an ordinary multiple-choice screen, interact with an answer label. On the hours question, interact with the slider. On a passage that is still revealing new words or choices, wait. These are different situations, and repeatedly clicking the empty area below the text will not solve all three.

You are not required to agree with it outside the game or to carry any instruction away from the screen.

sections.player_question: A house tour that changes its tone
sections.case_text: The Open House turns a familiar piece of online browsing into a short psychological horror game. Instead of arriving as an armed investigator, you enter a polished virtual property presentation. The apparent job is ordinary: look around a house, examine its rooms and understand what is being offered. That comfortable framing matters. A property tour encourages you to trust labels, interfaces and the person guiding the visit, so a change in those things feels different from a monster appearing in a place that already looked dangerous.

What input is available now? Answer those three questions before searching every other room. This keeps a small uncertainty from turning into a full restart. It also protects the pacing: the tour can build tension from waiting and looking, whereas constant clicking makes it harder to notice how the presentation is changing.

sections.heading: If the browser version does not start

A laptop or desktop also gives the tour more room for its interface than a narrow phone display. Do not expect a touch screen to reproduce an unconfirmed desktop input scheme. If a control lies outside the visible game area, enlarge the player or rotate the device before assuming that the game has no way forward.
